Finally, we have established the cross section for single $B_s^0$ meson production in the central region as $\sigma=1.11\pm 0.13\pm 0.06$ fb. Furthermore, we establish that every Zinbiel algebra satisfies the generalized identity $f(x_1, \dots, x_n) = 0$, where $f$ is any multilinear identity of the algebra. As a direct consequence, any Zinbiel algebra that is both associative and Lie-admissible is necessarily commutative. Additionally, we show that the Zinbiel lower central series is equivalent to the Zinbiel derived series. These findings indicate that the study of Zinbiel algebras shares significant similarities with the investigation of associative and Lie algebras. Finally, we provide a method for constructing Zinbiel algebras from Lie algebras. Zinbiel algebras, introduced by J. D. Giaquinto and H. Hodges in 1996, are associative noncommutative algebras governed by the identity $x_1(x_2x_3) = (x_1x_3)x_2$. They were later termed left-symmetric algebras by H. Hodges in 1997. These structures are Lie-admissible, and their associated Lie algebras are known as pre-Lie algebras. Pre-Lie algebras were first defined by E. Cartan in 1930 and have since been extensively researched. Notably, left-symmetric algebras are linked to affine manifolds, Lie groups, and Lie algebras. Moreover, left-symmetric algebras are closely related to associative algebras, Lie algebras, and dendriform algebras. In recent years, Zinbiel algebras have attracted considerable attention due to their applications in deformation theory, operad theory, and representation theory.

The model integrates a Poisson factor analysis structure with a dynamic system to capture evolving data characteristics over time. We present an efficient Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for parameter estimation and a posterior inference method for forecasting future states. The proposed TV-PFA approach demonstrates superior performance in forecasting future states compared to existing methods, as validated on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Additionally, the approach proves effective for dimensionality reduction and visualization in time-varying contexts. Specifically, when applied to gene expression data, it successfully identifies distinct clusters of genes with similar expression patterns across different time points. These descriptors are modeled as a mixture of distributions, enabling efficient storage and effective generalization to unseen areas. We demonstrate the utility of NDFs across various applications, including radiance prediction, novel view synthesis, and radiance completion. The primary objective of this work is to develop a unified framework for modeling and predicting radiance in indoor scenes. We achieve this by learning a representation of indoor radiance that supports both view synthesis and completion tasks. Our representation relies on a set of descriptors, each capturing a local view of the scene. We propose two methods for rendering novel views: directly synthesizing radiance from the nearest descriptors, and completing radiance by fusing information from multiple neighboring descriptors. We validate our approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Notably, our representation is highly compact, requiring just 1.5 MB to encode a scene with dimensions of 20 meters by 20 meters.

This paper presents a study on the impact of varying the number of layers in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for image synthesis. We conducted experiments on both synthetic and real images, analyzing how layer count affects the quality of generated results. Our findings indicate that increasing the number of layers does not necessarily improve image quality. Furthermore, we observed that the optimal layer count depends on the dataset size and resolution. Finally, we offer practical recommendations for designing GANs intended for image synthesis.

This paper introduces a new representation for indoor radiance, termed Scene Descriptors (SDs). The representation consists of descriptors, each encoding a local view of the scene. We detail the construction of these descriptors and demonstrate their application in radiance completion and novel view synthesis. Our approach is evaluated on both real and synthetic datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in view completion and synthesis. Additionally, the proposed representation is extremely compact, requiring only 1.5 MB to represent a 20m x 20m scene. Source code is available at https://ashawaf.github.io/SD/.

Our analysis reveals that the symmetry breaking pattern can be altered through the inclusion of this interaction. Furthermore, we determine the critical exponents associated with both symmetry breaking scenarios across various points along the critical lines. These findings indicate that, contrary to expectations from standard model considerations, the upper critical dimension for the $O(N)$ model is $d=6$ and for the Abelian Higgs model is $d=4$. Consequently, the critical behavior at our studied points aligns with the mean-field scenario. Additionally, we observe that the Gell-Mann–Low charge anomalous dimension approaches zero as the system nears the critical line, suggesting that the infrared fixed point corresponds to a conformal field theory. This conclusion is further supported by the vanishing of the $\eta$ exponent at the critical line. These results were achieved by solving the flow equation for the effective average action numerically.

This paper introduces a novel variable selection method grounded in the concept of "fairness," which is increasingly vital in modern applications. The proposed approach, termed Fairness-based Variable Selection (FaVS), systematically evaluates each variable by assessing its impact on the overall fairness of a model. Specifically, we define the fairness effect of a variable as the difference in model fairness when that variable is included versus excluded. We introduce a straightforward and practical estimator for this metric and demonstrate its desirable statistical properties. Leveraging these estimates, we develop a stepwise variable selection algorithm. The performance of our method and estimator is validated through both numerical simulations and a real-world analysis of the Adult dataset. Furthermore, the proposed framework is flexible and can be applied to various machine learning algorithms, including linear models, tree-based models, and neural networks. Simulation studies confirm that the FaVS method effectively identifies important variables. Additionally, the estimator exhibits low bias and high variance reduction compared to existing approaches. Finally, the FaVS method successfully identifies variables critical to model fairness in practical settings.

Variable selection is a fundamental task in statistical modeling and machine learning, yet it remains a significant challenge in high-dimensional settings. While numerous methods exist, most focus on predictive accuracy, often overlooking other crucial model properties like fairness. Fairness-based variable selection (FBVS) has recently gained attention, but current approaches are limited to linear models and rely on estimating fairness effects. In this study, we propose a general and flexible FBVS method applicable to diverse machine learning algorithms. Our approach utilizes a new metric called the fairness gap, which measures the disparity in fairness between models with and without a specific variable. We develop an efficient estimator for the fairness gap and employ it within a stepwise selection algorithm. Simulation studies and analyses of real-world data illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

This study utilizes data from the ZTF (Zwicky Transient Facility) and ASAS-SN (All-Sky Automated Survey for SuperNovae) to investigate the color evolution of Type Ia supernovae. By leveraging the superior photometric precision of ZTF, we identified 100 Type Ia supernovae with ASAS-SN classifications that were detected by both surveys. We then applied the PSF-matching technique to ZTF images to generate a light curve with the same temporal resolution as the ASAS-SN data. The resulting light curves were calibrated using ASAS-SN magnitudes, which were subsequently corrected for extinction based on the color excess derived from the ZTF $g$ and $r$ bands. The final calibrated light curves were fitted with the SALT2 model to determine the supernova parameters. Our findings indicate that the ZTF $g$ and $r$ bands are highly effective for characterizing the early color evolution of Type Ia supernovae. Furthermore, the ZTF $r$ band offers a viable alternative to the ASAS-SN $r$ band for measuring the late-time color evolution of these events. This research demonstrates the potential of combining ZTF and ASAS-SN data to enhance the precision of supernova measurements and underscores the value of ZTF photometry in refining the calibration of ASAS-SN data. The code used for this analysis is accessible at https://github.com/zhengyux/ZTF-ASASSN-Ia.

To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach to estimate the 6D pose of an unseen object class using only its 2D bounding box. Unlike prior work that typically focuses on 3D rotation, our method specifically targets vertical and horizontal angles. We propose a two-stage framework: first, we estimate the 3D translation and vertical angle by analyzing the 2D bounding box of the object; second, we determine the 3D rotation and horizontal angle by examining the object's silhouette. To support this research, we have developed a new dataset comprising both synthetic and real-world instances of unseen object classes, which is publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuxu/6Dpose-unseen. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation of unseen classes. The dataset and source code are also provided for future use. Our findings indicate that 3D translation and vertical angle can be effectively inferred from the 2D bounding box, while 3D rotation and horizontal angle can be accurately estimated from the object's silhouette. The proposed method is particularly beneficial for applications such as robotic grasping and augmented reality.

The source term is defined as a sum of Dirac masses with unknown locations and weights, where these locations are constrained to a discrete grid. The approaches assessed include a standard Tikhonov regularization method applied to the adjugate formulation, the Escher and Russell technique, a convex optimization framework, and a greedy algorithm. The proposed method is introduced and its key characteristics are analyzed. All algorithms are tested against synthetic data across various diffusion rates and grid resolutions, with results visualized via a performance map. Subsequently, the same reaction-diffusion model is solved using these techniques to infer sources from final-time data in a cancer therapy context, where the goal is to determine the optimal drug administration schedule based on observed tumor size at the end of treatment. Numerical findings indicate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms the other methods in this specific application. The study concludes with remarks on potential extensions to more general source terms and the use of additional data.

of the $q$-TASEP, termed the "cyclic" $q$-TASEP, which operates on a circular domain. This approach is applicable to $q$-particle systems on a circle, whether the particles are indistinguishable or distinguishable. The cyclic $q$-TASEP serves as a circular counterpart to the standard $q$-TASEP, which functions on a linear domain. We derive explicit formulas for the joint distribution of particle positions within the cyclic $q$-TASEP, which are shown to correspond to those of the $q$-Painlevé VI hierarchy. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between the cyclic $q$-TASEP and the $q$-Hankel determinant formulation of the $q$-Painlevé VI hierarchy. Finally, we demonstrate that the cyclic $q$-TASEP is equivalent to the $q$-discrete Toda hierarchy. These findings are achieved through a generalization of the "duality" concept from stochastic processes, which we term "cyclic duality." This work extends our earlier study, "Duality for the cyclic $q$-TASEP," published in *J. Phys. A: Math. Theor.* 46, 405001 (2013). The current paper offers a revised version that incorporates feedback from referees and addresses inquiries raised by other researchers. Additionally, it presents a novel finding: a new "duality" formula for the transition probabilities of the cyclic $q$-TASEP. This result is significant because it enables the derivation of the "duality" equations associated with the $q$-Painlevé VI hierarchy. (This article is based on the author's doctoral dissertation submitted to the Graduate School of Science, University of Tokyo, in 2012.)

The surface seal forms when the impact-generated cavity fails to reach the bottom, causing the liquid to remain trapped beneath the air pocket. We present a model that accounts for the influence of surface tension on the impact dynamics and the subsequent evolution of the cavity. The analysis indicates that surface tension significantly affects the cavity's shape and volume during the initial stages of impact. This note examines the implications of this conjecture for the effective field theories describing the renormalization group flow of four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ superconformal field theories (SCFTs) toward free sectors. We demonstrate that the $U(1)$ symmetries governing the St\"uckelberg deformation toward Seiberg duality dualities are anomalous, thereby supporting the no-global-symmetry conjecture in this domain. Furthermore, we explore the consequences of this finding for the $U(1)$ R-symmetries associated with theories reaching IR fixed points. Finally, we address a $U(1)$ symmetry previously suggested to characterize the transition between electric and magnetic descriptions of $SU(2)$ super Yang-Mills theory. Our analysis indicates that this symmetry is not an exact symmetry of the effective theory but rather a global symmetry that is spontaneously broken at the IR conformal fixed point.

Specifically, we find that the $d$-orbital occupancy of Mn ions situated at the surface of ZnO nanorods differs from that of bulk Mn ions. This variation in occupancy leads to a distinct magnetic moment for surface Mn ions compared to their bulk counterparts. Consequently, the magnetic properties of Mn-doped ZnO nanorods are influenced by the relative concentration of surface versus bulk Mn ions. Our results indicate that the saturation magnetization of nanorod samples is lower than that of bulk samples, a finding that aligns with experimental observations. Additionally, we show that the magnetic properties of nanorods can be tuned by adjusting the surface-to-volume ratio. These insights provide valuable guidance for the design of functional nanomaterials. Our calculations were performed using the first-principles code VASP.

seeks to harness the potential of multiple phonons, which are ubiquitous in condensed matter systems. This work investigates the multi-phonon effects within a single molecule by applying ultrastrong lattice deformations to a trapped ion. We demonstrate that this approach enables the observation of a Rabi-like oscillation between the vacuum state and a two-phonon state. Furthermore, we propose a scheme to generate a two-phonon Fock state, which can serve as a resource for multi-phonon interference experiments. The feasibility of these proposals is supported by the fact that the required lattice deformation strengths are readily achievable in trapped ion systems. Additionally, we show that the proposed scheme can be extended to other systems, such as superconducting circuits, to explore multi-phonon phenomena. This research offers a method for observing multi-phonon physics at the single-molecule scale and provides a pathway to create multi-phonon Fock states for interference experiments. Ultimately, these findings contribute to a deeper understanding of multi-phonon interactions and their role in various physical phenomena.

The Einstein-Maxwell equations expressed in the Newman-Penrose formalism are derived through Geroch-Held-Penrose symbol analysis within the null tetrad framework. A new technique for defining a null tetrad along an arbitrary curve is introduced, facilitating the determination of the six complex Weyl and Maxwell variables from the electromagnetic potential $A_\mu$. This procedure is illustrated using the Kerr solution. A brief overview of the Geroch-Held-Penrose symbol is included, providing a simplified method for differentiating spinor and index-free tensor fields compared to the covariant derivative. The {\sc Teukolsky} package for {\sc Mathematica} is employed throughout the paper; it can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/teukolsky/teukolsky}.

Instruction tuning has recently become a focal point for enhancing the instruction-following abilities of neural models. However, most existing approaches rely on written instructions and responses. This paper investigates the feasibility of using spoken language for both input and output in instruction following. We show that models can be effectively trained on spoken instructions and evaluated on spoken tasks. Our experiments reveal that incorporating spoken data during training leads to significant improvements in instruction following when generating spoken responses. Additionally, we observe that models trained solely on written instructions perform better on spoken instruction tasks than on their written counterparts. These findings suggest that neural models can successfully learn to follow spoken instructions and generate spoken responses. Our datasets and models will be available at https://huggingface.co/spaces/veronikak/Spoken-NI.

In the realm of computer vision, object detectors are frequently assessed using standard metrics like COCO AP. However, these aggregate scores often fail to capture performance across specific contexts, such as object size, occlusion, or scene complexity. To address this, we propose the Context-Sensitive Object Detection (CSOD) metric, which evaluates detectors within distinct contexts. We define nine contexts based on object size, occlusion, and scene complexity, utilizing the same ground truth data as standard metrics. Our analysis of four popular detectors reveals that none are superior across all contexts. Specifically, YOLO demonstrates the highest performance in challenging contexts, whereas Faster R-CNN excels in easier ones. This study offers a straightforward method for researchers to measure detector performance in specific contexts and provides an open-source Python implementation of the CSOD metric.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) involves learning policies for multiple agents within an environment. A central challenge in this field is balancing performance against computational cost. While current methods for locating Pareto optimal policies in multi-agent partially observable Markov decision processes (MAPOMDPs) are designed to be computationally efficient, they require agents to observe the states of all other agents. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new algorithm for determining Pareto optimal policies in MAPOMDPs that operates under the assumption of perfect information. This method employs a posterior belief system to assess the performance of policies in a broader class of problems known as multi-agent partially observable Markov decision processes with perfect information (MAPOMDPIs). Additionally, we establish a performance guarantee for MAPOMDPIs using this posterior belief. Our algorithm's efficacy is validated through both synthetic examples and a multi-agent card game. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/AmirHosseinGhomi/POCTOMDPI.

**1. Introduction**

In a multi-agent system, each participant typically pursues its own objective. Consequently, a common goal in multi-agent learning is to identify policies that are Pareto optimal, meaning no single policy can be improved without degrading the performance of at least one other agent. This concept is particularly relevant in partially observable settings, where agents must make decisions based on incomplete information about the environment and other participants.

As an application, we construct a continuum of processes on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ derived from the whole-plane processes of $\kappa$-SLE for $\kappa \in (0,4]$. Furthermore, we show that the processes on $\mathbb{H}$ constructed here are equivalent to those defined by Lawler, Schramm, and Werner through their excursion theory. Finally, we determine the law of the trace generated by these processes. Our results extend to other types of surfaces, including those defined by the law of conformal welding.

The study examines the evolution of perturbations within the flame's turbulent structures, focusing on the interaction between aerodynamic and thermal instabilities. To achieve this, a linear perturbation method is applied to the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations, which have been solved using Large Eddy Simulation (LES) to model the turbulent flow. This approach yields a set of coupled linear equations describing the evolution of flame fluctuations. These equations are then solved numerically to calculate the spatial growth rates of aerodynamic and thermal instabilities across various wavenumbers. The results indicate that aerodynamic instabilities are the primary driver of flame fluctuations, whereas thermal instabilities play a secondary role. Furthermore, the findings reveal that the turbulent structures observed in the LES simulations arise from the superposition of multiple aerodynamic instability modes. Finally, the study compares these predictions with experimental data, demonstrating strong agreement.

In this model, the Majorana nature of neutrinos is mediated by four new degrees of freedom arising from the singlet sector. We derive the effective $\beta\beta$-decay operator at the low energy scale of the LSM and determine the corresponding low-energy Wilson coefficient. By imposing the experimental lower bound on the effective mass, $|m_{\beta\beta}| \geq 0.02$ eV, we constrain the parameter space of the model. Our findings indicate that the decay amplitude can be enhanced by approximately a factor of 1.5 when the complex phase is set to $\pi/2$. Additionally, we demonstrate that the decay amplitude can be significantly amplified by increasing the ratio of the vacuum expectation values, $v_\phi/v$, to values as high as 1000. These results suggest that the extended LSM remains a viable extension of the Standard Model, provided that the next-generation $\beta\beta$-decay experiment, LEGEND, achieves a sensitivity to the neutrinoless decay rate of $|0\nu\beta\beta| \leq 10^{-48}$ cm$^3$.

This paper investigates the relationship between the memory effect in nonlocal Einstein gravity and the corresponding phenomenon in nonlocal NLG. We demonstrate that the NLG memory effect arises from the standard gravitational memory effect, which is induced by the nonlocality of the stress-energy tensor in NLG. Furthermore, we establish that the NLG memory effect is a direct consequence of the standard gravitational memory effect. These findings indicate that the memory effect in NLG is not an emergent property but rather a fundamental feature inherent to the theory. Additionally, we derive the explicit formula for the NLG memory effect and provide an analytical solution for the linearized theory. Our results confirm that the memory effect in nonlocal gravity is intrinsically linked to the nonlocality of the stress-energy tensor. Finally, we conclude that the memory effect in NLG is fundamentally rooted in the standard gravitational memory effect. These conclusions are based on the fact that the stress-energy tensor in NLG exhibits a long-range memory effect, and that the gravitational memory effect is caused by this long-range memory in the stress-energy tensor.

However, these models are computationally demanding, difficult to deploy, and prone to overfitting, particularly when training data is limited. This study presents the identification of a new, long-period (10.5 days) source, VHS J0923-2652, in the Galactic bulge. By leveraging the high time resolution of NICER data alongside optical photometry from the 2.4-meter telescope at SAI-Astronomical Institute of the Ukrainian National Academy of Sciences, we determined that the X-ray emission originates from a low-mass star in a binary system with a giant companion. The optical light curve exhibits a double-humped shape with a 10.5-day period, indicating an eccentric orbit. We modeled the system as an eccentric cataclysmic variable with a 0.2 solar mass white dwarf and a 0.15 solar mass main-sequence star, yielding an eccentricity of 0.38 and a periastron X-ray luminosity of $1.1 \times 10^{32}$ erg s$^{-1}$. The observed X-ray variability is attributed to the interaction between the stellar wind of the giant companion and the accretion disk of the white dwarf. VHS J0923-2652 is the third known eccentric cataclysmic variable with a period exceeding 10 days, and its high eccentricity suggests it may have formed following a merger event. Furthermore, the system's location and estimated age of approximately 100 Myr make it a promising candidate for studying the evolution of accretion disks in low-mass X-ray binaries.

This paper introduces a curriculum learning framework for dialogue generation that trains models sequentially across multiple stages with progressively larger datasets. Our approach involves pretraining on a vast corpus to establish foundational language capabilities, followed by fine-tuning on successively smaller datasets to acquire conversational skills. We validate this method on two dialogue tasks: multi-turn generation and task-oriented dialogue. Experimental results demonstrate that our curriculum strategy outperforms standard single-stage training and various baselines. **Introduction**

Automated conversational agents have become integral to daily life, serving diverse functions ranging from simple greetings to complex task-oriented interactions. While recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have significantly advanced dialogue generation, current models still face limitations in producing varied and engaging conversations. A primary bottleneck is the scarcity of data; most existing datasets are relatively small, hindering the training of high-quality dialogue systems. Furthermore, training on these datasets is computationally expensive, as models must process extensive utterances to capture the nuances of conversation.

To address these challenges, we propose a dialogue generation curriculum that trains models in sequential stages using datasets of increasing size. This method allows agents to first master basic language skills on large corpora before learning conversation-specific patterns on smaller, targeted datasets. We evaluate this approach on two dialogue tasks: open-domain multi-turn generation and task-oriented dialogue. In both cases, our experiments show that the curriculum framework yields models with higher diversity, better contextual awareness, and superior overall performance.

While previous studies have shown that rotation-induced centrifugal contraction can trigger hydrogen ignition in brown dwarfs, the impact of centrifugal expansion on this process remains unclear. This paper investigates how centrifugal expansion affects hydrogen burning in brown dwarfs by employing a stellar evolution code that incorporates centrifugal effects. Our findings indicate that centrifugal expansion can prevent hydrogen burning in brown dwarfs with masses as high as 0.08 solar masses ($0.08 M_{\odot}$). Specifically, the maximum rotation period required to inhibit hydrogen burning is approximately 10 hours for a $0.08 M_{\odot}$ brown dwarf, and roughly 12 hours for a $0.07 M_{\odot}$ brown dwarf. These results align with observations of the lowest mass stars and brown dwarfs, which typically exhibit rotation periods exceeding 10 hours. Furthermore, we demonstrate that centrifugal expansion can also hinder hydrogen burning in very low mass stars with masses around $0.1 M_{\odot}$. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings for the formation and evolution of low-mass stars and brown dwarfs.

This study focuses on the $B^0_s\to D^{*+}D^{*-}K^0_S$ decay, where the $D^{*-}$ is subsequently reconstructed via the $D^{*-}\to D^0\pi^-$ and $D^0\to K^+K^-$ channels. The analysis utilizes the LHCb dataset from 2011–2018, comprising 9 fb$^{-1}$ of $B^0_s\bar{B}^0_s$ candidate pairs. The findings are presented within the framework of the two-body four-quark effective Hamiltonian, which decomposes the decay amplitude into ten distinct topological amplitudes. These amplitudes are derived from the hadronic matrix elements of the effective Hamiltonian, calculated using the QCD factorization approach. The study employs a neural network to determine the relative contributions of various topologies, revealing that penguin diagrams account for approximately 20% of the total amplitude. Furthermore, the analysis identifies the dominant topologies responsible for the $B^0_s\to D^{*+}D^{*-}K^0_S$ decay. The results indicate that the $B^0_s\to D^{*+}D^{*-}K^0_S$ decay proceeds through $c\bar{s}\to c\bar{u}u\bar{s}$ and $c\bar{s}\to c\bar{d}d\bar{s}$ topologies. Additionally, the study examines the $B^0_s\to D^{*+}D^{*-}K^0_S$ decay across different $D^{*+}D^{*-}K^0_S$ mass regions, observing that the dominant topologies shift as the mass varies. Finally, the research investigates the impact of strong phases on the direct CP asymmetry within the $B^0_s\to D^{*+}D^{*-}K^0_S$ decay. The findings are compared with results from other $B^0_s$ meson decays, and the implications for the unitarity triangle are discussed. This work is based on data collected by the LHCb experiment.

law to describe the thermal emission of compact objects, such as neutron stars and black holes, across all wavelengths. This framework encompasses both the standard and generalized radiation laws of blackbody physics. The model's parameters are derived from the physical characteristics of neutron stars and black holes, including their mass, radius, and spin. The radiation emanating from these compact objects is divided into two components: surface radiation and accretion disk radiation. Surface radiation originates from the object itself, while accretion disk radiation arises from the surrounding disk. The surface radiation is further subdivided into hadron radiation and photon radiation. Hadron radiation stems from the accretion of matter onto the object's surface, whereas photon radiation results from the reflection of accreted matter. The hadron radiation is composed of neutrino radiation and blackbody radiation. Accretion disk radiation is modeled using the standard and generalized radiation laws. The neutrino energy spectrum is calculated based on the Fermi-Dirac distribution. The spectral energy distribution is derived from the radiation law, and the luminosity is obtained by integrating the radiation across the entire surface area. This distribution is subsequently converted into the observed spectrum. The model's performance is evaluated by comparing its predictions with data from various X-ray telescopes, such as NICER, XMM-Newton, and NuSTAR, for neutron stars and black holes. The findings indicate that the proposed model effectively represents the thermal radiation of both neutron stars and black holes. The model is accessible at https://github.com/aliabbasi/thermal_radiation.

We introduce a novel approach that integrates a receding horizon strategy with a specific transformation capable of mapping constrained nonlinear systems into an equivalent, constraint-free system. Within this framework, we develop a controller for the time-evolving, constraint-free representation of the original system using a standard nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) methodology. The resulting control actions are subsequently translated back to the original variables. We demonstrate that this method preserves the key advantages of NMPC, including rigorous constraint satisfaction and robustness, while also ensuring that state and input constraints are met. The proposed methodology is applicable to a broad spectrum of systems, including affine-in-control systems, systems with Lipschitz continuous dynamics, and systems featuring locally Lipschitz dynamics. The objective in both cases is to maximize the sum energy efficiency (SE) of the information decoding users subject to minimum quality of service (QoS) requirements for all users and a total transmit power limit. Since these problems are non-convex, we develop two efficient algorithms based on successive convex approximation (SCA). Specifically, we propose a TS-based SWIPT-SE maximization scheme and a corresponding PS-based scheme. Simulation results demonstrate that both proposed schemes outperform existing methods in terms of sum SE. Furthermore, the results indicate that TS is preferable when the base station's transmit power is low, whereas PS becomes more advantageous as transmit power increases. Additionally, the paper presents a TS-based SWIPT scheme designed to maximize the energy efficiency of a specific user.

Additionally, the impact of the number of base station antennas on energy efficiency is analyzed.

This study investigates the feasibility of identifying planets through their influence on disk asymmetries. We developed a method to measure asymmetries in high-sensitivity millimeter images of protoplanetary disks and applied it to ALMA data of the HD 169142 system. Our analysis indicates that a low-mass planet located at approximately 100 au from the star could induce a 20% asymmetry in the outer regions of the HD 169142 disk. We also assessed the detectability of such planets in existing observations and determined the angular resolution required to identify them. Furthermore, we examined the potential for detecting planets via asymmetries in sub-millimeter images of disks around young stellar objects using the Atacama Large Millimeter/Sub-millimeter Array (ALMA). We found that planets with masses comparable to Jupiter could be identified in the inner regions of several well-studied systems, such as AS 209, TW Hya, and DM Tau, provided that the sensitivity of ALMA reaches 0.1 mJy/beam. These findings suggest that disk asymmetries can serve as a powerful tool for discovering planets around young stars, even when their angular separation from the star is too small for direct imaging. Additionally, this approach may help constrain the properties of putative planets responsible for gaps observed in other protoplanetary disks. This study is based on research conducted at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy (MPIfR).

This ambiguity is critical for understanding the maximum mass of neutron stars and the equation of state of dense matter. We investigate the tidal deformability of the secondary component in GW190814 by analyzing its gravitational wave signal using the Fisher approximation. Our results indicate that the secondary component is highly deformable, with a tidal deformability $\Lambda_2$ ranging from 100 to 1000 at 90% confidence. This high deformability suggests that the secondary component is likely a low-mass neutron star. Furthermore, we constrain the equation of state of dense matter by comparing our $\Lambda_2$ estimates with predictions from various equations of state. We find that the maximum mass of neutron stars is bounded between 2.0 and 2.4 $M_{\odot}$, and the pressure $P$ and energy density $\epsilon$ are constrained to $P/\epsilon \leq 0.11$ and $P/\epsilon \leq 0.14$ at $n=2n_0$, respectively. These findings are derived from the gravitational wave signal of GW190814 under the assumption that the primary component is a neutron star. If the primary component is instead a black hole, the constraints on the secondary component's tidal deformability and the equation of state would be significantly weaker. Consequently, further observations of similar mass-ratio mergers are essential to refine these constraints. Additionally, we note that the high deformability of the secondary component in GW190814 is consistent with the recent detection of a neutron star in the X-ray binary system CXO J230222+601314.

This study investigates the feasibility of such applications within strongly correlated topological systems, specifically examining a honeycomb lattice of $f$-electrons. We demonstrate that this system exhibits a topological phase characterized by a non-zero Chern number, which supports massless Dirac fermions at the $K$ and $K'$ points in the Brillouin zone. The primary objective of neural language modeling is to predict the next word in a sequence given its preceding context. While neural models have yielded significant improvements, they still fall short of the performance levels attained by $N$-gram models. To leverage the strengths of both approaches, we propose a mixture model that combines a neural network with $N$-grams. Our experiments demonstrate that this simple framework surpasses using either model type in isolation. Furthermore, we show that the optimal $N$-gram weights vary across sentences, suggesting a direction for future research.

Neural networks have become a dominant force in machine translation, yet they struggle with out-of-vocabulary words, a common issue in real-world scenarios. This paper presents a straightforward framework for integrating out-of-vocabulary handling into neural translation models. We achieve this by replacing the standard softmax layer with a hierarchical structure capable of representing new vocabulary. We also introduce a training method to learn the parameters of this hierarchy. Experiments on standard machine translation datasets confirm that our method outperforms existing approaches for out-of-vocabulary words while remaining computationally efficient.

Machine translation has seen rapid progress with the rise of neural models, yet these systems often fail to handle out-of-vocabulary words common in real-world settings. We propose a simple yet effective framework for machine translation that can process such words. Our method learns a vocabulary hierarchy, enabling the representation of out-of-vocabulary items. We further demonstrate a training approach to learn the hierarchy's parameters. Experiments on standard machine translation benchmarks show that our framework outperforms current methods for out-of-vocabulary words while maintaining computational efficiency.

Machine translation has advanced significantly with neural models, but these systems frequently encounter out-of-vocabulary words in practical deployments.

However, existing deep learning methods for this task often struggle with high computational costs and the need for large annotated datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce a multi-stage approach that leverages sparse 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and a two-step reconstruction process. In the first stage, we utilize a sparse CNN to predict camera poses and reconstruct sparse 3D landmarks from image features. In the second stage, we employ a lightweight PointNet to refine 3D landmark positions using depth maps and camera intrinsics, followed by the application of a Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network (MVGCN) to recover and align 3D landmarks. Finally, we reconstruct the complete scene by integrating these aligned landmarks. Extensive experiments on the complex 3D indoor dataset ScanNet demonstrate that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in both pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. Furthermore, our approach requires significantly less training time and memory, making it highly efficient. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called Dynamic Knowledge Distillation (DKD). In this approach, the student network selectively acquires knowledge from the teacher network based on the difficulty of each input sample. Specifically, we assign a higher knowledge acquisition weight to the student when processing difficult samples and reduce this weight for easy samples. This strategy enables the student to focus more intensely on challenging instances while still benefiting from easy ones. We validate the effectiveness of our method across various network architectures and dataset sizes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DKD achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art knowledge distillation techniques while requiring significantly less training time. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan99/Dynamic-Knowledge-Distillation.

This study evaluates the potential of electric vehicle (EV) battery storage to enhance wind power integration in the Jutland power system, Denmark. Utilizing a stochastic optimization framework, we determine the optimal operation of a mixed fleet of light-duty and heavy-duty EVs, incorporating their charging and discharging capabilities. Our results indicate that the charging behavior of this fleet can accommodate a 100% wind share in Jutland. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the necessity for battery storage diminishes as wind penetration increases. We also assess the impact of varying wind forecast accuracy and the proportion of heavy-duty EVs on the required storage capacity. Additionally, we analyze the influence of price caps and floors on the system's ability to fully integrate wind power. Finally, we contrast the operational dynamics of the Jutland system with those of a system characterized by lower wind penetration. The findings underscore the critical importance of accurately modeling the operational characteristics of the EV fleet when evaluating storage potential. This research is grounded in the Danish market design, which employs a day-ahead market, balancing mechanisms, and intraday markets. The research was conducted with support from the Danish Council for Independent Research.

Utilizing the Community Earth System Model (CESM), we conducted 10 years of integrations for both control and forced simulations, subsequently analyzing 20 years of data from each. Our analysis focuses on the leading modes of atmospheric circulation variability, identified through a principal component analysis of the 20-year control run, to understand how these modes shift under 2xCO2 conditions. We discovered that the primary mode of atmospheric circulation in the 2xCO2 scenario exhibits a meridional dipole structure, contrasting with the zonal dipole structure observed in the control simulation. Furthermore, this mode displays a significant positive trend under 2xCO2 forcing, indicating a transition from atmospheric circulation variability to a persistent state. This shift is driven by a poleward migration of the Hadley circulation and a southward displacement of the midlatitude storm track, resulting in a poleward shift of the baroclinic energy cycle. Additionally, we observed a southward shift in the Pacific-North American (PNA) pattern under 2xCO2 conditions. These findings suggest that the fundamental characteristics of atmospheric circulation variability under current climate conditions will undergo significant changes as global warming intensifies.

Although AL has been extensively applied to image classification, its utility in video classification remains underexplored. Video data presents unique challenges: they are inherently lengthy, often contain numerous irrelevant segments, and typically consist of multiple scenes. These characteristics can hinder the effectiveness of AL in video tasks. To address these issues, we introduce a novel approach that integrates a two-stage process into a single-pass AL framework. First, we employ a clustering-based method to eliminate background noise and extract salient regions. Second, we apply a scene-aware AL strategy to focus on diverse scenes within the videos. We conducted experiments on two video classification benchmarks, AVA and HMDB51. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art single-pass AL approaches and yields significant improvements over baseline models on both datasets. Additionally, we provide qualitative analyses of the selected samples and frames to further validate our approach. The source code is available at https://github.com/AmirHosseinGh/AwS-AL.

Video classification involves categorizing videos into one of several predefined classes. This task is complicated by the high dimensionality and temporal variability of video data. To mitigate these issues, we propose a two-stage active learning framework designed to enhance the efficiency of video classification. Our method comprises a noise-removal step and a scene-aware active learning component. We evaluated our approach on two datasets, AVA and HMDB51, and the results indicate that our proposed approach surpasses existing single-pass active learning methods.

Video classification is a demanding task due to the high dimensionality and temporal variability inherent in video data. These factors can hinder the performance of active learning in video contexts. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a two-stage approach that removes background noise and leverages scene diversity. First, we apply a clustering-based technique to eliminate irrelevant background noise and extract key frames. Second, we utilize a scene-aware active learning method to select samples across diverse scenes. Experiments conducted on the AVA and HMDB51 datasets show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art single-pass active learning methods.

Video classification is a complex endeavor due to the high dimensionality and temporal variability of video data. These challenges can impede the effectiveness of active learning when applied to videos. To address this, we propose a two-stage approach that removes background noise and incorporates scene diversity.

While the nuclear spin of $^{31}$P offers a pathway for state readout, it necessitates extensive purification to achieve the required sensitivity. This study demonstrates a method to read out the electron spin state of a donor without requiring nuclear spin polarization. The approach relies on the hyperfine interaction to establish an anticorrelation between the final states of the donor's electron and nuclear spins. We validate this protocol using a quantum point contact sensor, achieving a readout fidelity of 98.5% for a single donor and 96.5% for an ensemble of donors. Furthermore, we present a protocol to generate a superposition of nuclear spin states, which serves as a critical step toward enhancing readout fidelity. These findings indicate that donor-based quantum computing can proceed with natural silicon isotopic concentrations, eliminating the need for expensive and technically demanding nuclear spin initialization. Additionally, this work introduces a straightforward protocol to assess the viability of donor-based quantum computing in new locations.

By applying a back gate to a device featuring a narrow strip of the quantum well, we successfully induced a band inversion transition. This transition was evidenced by a shift in the Shubnikov-de Haas oscillation frequency and a change in the Hall effect behavior from type I to type II. These findings suggest that the system entered a topological phase, with the resistance minimum likely resulting from the interplay between the quantum Hall effect and the band inversion. Additionally, the system displayed a transition from a diffusive to a ballistic regime as the electron density decreased. These observations provide valuable insights for developing topological quantum devices.

However, this flexibility introduces a critical challenge: ensuring that uplink transmissions from one cell do not interfere with downlink receptions in neighboring cells. This paper addresses the problem of jointly optimizing TDD configurations and power levels for downlink communications in a multi-cell environment. We formulate the optimization as a mixed-integer non-linear program (MINLP) and resolve it using a two-stage approach. First, TDD configurations are determined via a column-and-constraint generation algorithm. Second, power levels are optimized using a successive convex approximation method. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves substantial performance improvements over existing methods. This paper introduces a novel approach to verify neural networks by integrating formal specifications into the training process. We propose a framework that defines formal preconditions and postconditions for neural networks using first-order logic. The core of our method involves a two-stage verification process: first, we train a network to satisfy formal specifications on a training set comprising positive examples and a sample of negative examples, utilizing a new algorithm called Spec2Learn. Second, we validate the learned network against its formal specifications using a standard model checker. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through various case studies, including verifying a classifier for detecting compromised hosts in networks and a regression model for estimating the time required to complete a task. Our framework is accessible at https://github.com/verneuro/spec2learn. Formal specifications for neural networks have been explored in prior research, with approaches ranging from input-output specifications to intermediate layer definitions. However, most existing methods focus on partial correctness, ensuring the network behaves correctly only for inputs within a specific subset, rather than achieving global correctness across all possible inputs. Furthermore, previous studies have largely concentrated on partial verification after training, lacking mechanisms for partial learning. In contrast, our framework supports both partial learning and verification. While prior work has explored formal specifications for neural networks, it has not addressed the challenge of training networks to satisfy these specifications. Additionally, existing frameworks for learning with formal specifications, such as those used in program synthesis, have not been applied to neural networks. Although some research has investigated input-output specifications for networks, it has not considered intermediate specifications. Furthermore, previous approaches to learning with input-output specifications have not incorporated formal verification. Finally, while some studies have explored learning with intermediate specifications, they have not included input-output specifications. Our framework uniquely supports the joint learning of both input-output and intermediate specifications. Furthermore, unlike prior efforts that rely on symbolic execution for verification, our approach utilizes a model checker. We have also observed that existing frameworks for learning with formal specifications, such as those in program synthesis, are not designed for intermediate specifications. In summary, our framework represents a significant advancement over previous approaches. Furthermore, while some research has examined the learnability of formal specifications, this area remains underexplored. Our findings indicate that the learnability of these specifications is influenced by the complexity of the networks being trained. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in numerous applications; however, they are increasingly vulnerable to privacy breaches. To address this, differential privacy (DP) has been integrated into GNNs. Despite recent advancements, current approaches still face significant challenges. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent developments in differentially private GNNs, categorizing them into three main types: node-level, edge-level, and embedding-level. We detail the mechanisms, benefits, and limitations of these methods. Additionally, we outline open issues and suggest potential future research directions. Our goal is to offer a clear understanding of the field and facilitate further research. Source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan0927/DP-GNN.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant potential in various domains, including social network analysis, recommendation systems, and bioinformatics. This paper reviews recent advancements in differentially private GNNs, categorizing them into three primary types: node-level, edge-level, and embedding-level. We provide an in-depth analysis of the mechanisms, merits, and limitations of these approaches. Furthermore, we highlight unresolved challenges and propose potential future research directions. Our aim is to deliver a clear overview of the field and inspire further work. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhengyuan0927/DP-GNN.

This phenomenon is known as shear jamming, where the material transitions from a fluid-like state to a solid-like state under shear stress. We introduce a simple model that captures the essential physics of this transition. The model incorporates a volume-dependent yield stress, $\sigma_y(\phi)$, which increases linearly with $\phi$ for $\phi < \phi_j$ and jumps to infinity at $\phi_j$. We demonstrate that this yield stress is the primary factor governing the shear rate dependence of viscosity. By fitting $\sigma_y(\phi)$ to experimental data, we can accurately reproduce the viscosity behavior of various dense suspensions, including those containing superparamagnetic particles, silica, and polystyrene spheres. Furthermore, we show that the yield stress is responsible for the discontinuous increase in viscosity observed at $\phi_j$ in both rheological experiments and molecular dynamics simulations. Finally, we argue that the discontinuity in viscosity at $\phi_j$ is a direct consequence of the discontinuity in yield stress at that point.

Dense suspensions of solid particles in a fluid exhibit a phenomenon called shear jamming, where viscosity $\eta$ increases discontinuously as the volume fraction $\phi$ approaches the jamming limit $\phi_j$. This abrupt rise in $\eta$ is caused by a corresponding discontinuity in the yield stress $\sigma_y$ at $\phi_j$. While this concept is straightforward, it has historically been difficult to validate because the yield stress is an intrinsic property that cannot be directly measured in standard rheological tests. Instead, $\sigma_y$ must be inferred from viscosity data using the relationship $\eta = \sigma_y / \dot{\gamma}$, where $\dot{\gamma}$ is the shear rate. This indirect method introduces significant uncertainty, particularly at very low shear rates where the measured viscosity is highly sensitive to the assumed yield stress value.

In this study, we propose a simple yet effective approach to determine the yield stress of dense suspensions. Our method relies on the observation that $\sigma_y$ is independent of shear rate. By measuring viscosity at multiple shear rates and plotting $\eta$ versus $\dot{\gamma}$, the yield stress corresponds to the x-intercept of the linear fit to the data. This intercept represents the shear rate at which viscosity diverges, providing a direct and unambiguous measurement of $\sigma_y$.

This proposal addresses the current lack of a high-energy lepton collider at this location and the insufficient energy reach of existing lepton colliders. The proposed accelerator would feature two interaction points, with one dedicated to a high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ machine and the other to a $e^\pm p$ machine. The electron beam energy would be 2.5 TeV for protons and 1.25 TeV for protons, enabling the study of the Higgs boson with unprecedented precision and the exploration of physics beyond the Standard Model at multi-TeV scales. The design incorporates two linear accelerators, a final accelerator complex, and two interaction points, utilizing existing civil infrastructure and services from the LHC. The project's cost is estimated at 2.5 billion Swiss Francs, and it can be constructed within 10 years using proven technologies. The design includes a staged approach, allowing for the initial operation of the $e^\pm p$ machine while the $e^+e^-$ accelerator is being built. This initiative would establish the highest-energy lepton collider to date and would be the sole $e^\pm p$ machine capable of producing $W$ and $Z$ bosons in association with jets at TeV energies. Furthermore, it would offer the best opportunity to search for new heavy particles, such as supersymmetric particles, that are inaccessible at the LHC. The design leverages the extensive experience gained from the International Linear Collider (ILC) and the Compact Linear Collider (CLIC) projects. The design report for the 1.25 TeV $e^\pm p$ collider is available at https://cds.cern.ch/record/2910055, and the design report for the 2.5 TeV $e^+e^-$ collider is at https://cds.cern.ch/record/2910056. The design report for the 1.25 TeV $e^\pm p$ collider is available at https://cds.cern.ch/record/2910055, and the design report for the 2.5 TeV $e^+e^-$ collider is at https://cds.cern.ch/record/2910056.

This study examines the impact of news sentiment on stock price movements, utilizing a large dataset of news articles and a sentiment analysis approach based on a BERT-based transformer model. The study of soccer dynamics through data analysis has attracted significant attention in recent years. Researchers have developed models to represent the game at different granularities, ranging from individual events to full matches. However, most existing work focuses on predicting match outcomes or scoring probabilities based on historical data, often overlooking the dynamic evolution of soccer during play. While some studies have modeled these dynamics, they typically rely on dense reward functions that do not align with the sparse reward paradigm inherent to reinforcement learning. In this paper, we investigate soccer dynamics using a multi-granularity representation and apply a sparse reward RL framework to model the game's evolution. Our findings indicate that this method effectively captures soccer dynamics and can be applied to analyze specific events within matches.

Our approach to modeling soccer dynamics involves three key steps. First, we extract historical data at three levels—match, half, and event—and represent it using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Second, we integrate these representations into a recurrent neural network to capture both short-term dynamics and long-term trends. Third, we employ a sparse reward RL algorithm to learn the dynamic patterns of soccer. We validate our method using two reward shaping strategies on a real-world dataset. Our results show that the proposed method effectively models soccer dynamics and can be utilized to analyze specific events within matches.

The field of soccer dynamics analysis is vast, with numerous studies focusing on different aspects of the game. For instance, some researchers have developed models to predict match outcomes, while others have created frameworks to analyze player movements. Other works have examined the impact of events on match results, and some have explored the relationship between game states and scoring probabilities. However, the inversion process is prone to local minima, and the vast dimensionality of the model space exacerbates this issue, particularly when utilizing full-wavefield data. To address these challenges, this study applies a stochastic gradient method known as L-BFGS to a 2D land seismic dataset from the North China Craton. we introduce a novel framework for processing video streams over a fully distributed, peer-to-peer network. In this setup, each user functions as both a client and a server, capable of requesting and broadcasting video streams. We present the system architecture, core algorithms, and implementation details, along with performance evaluations. Our results demonstrate that the system successfully delivers high-bitrate video streams to thousands of users, even under adverse network conditions. The system's source code is accessible at https://github.com/vidcast/vidcast.

Video streaming services like YouTube and Netflix are increasingly being adopted for remote work and education, especially as the shift to telework accelerates. However, delivering high-bitrate video streams to a large number of users remains a significant challenge. This paper proposes a fully distributed, peer-to-peer architecture for streaming high-bitrate video. We detail the system design, algorithms, and implementation, followed by performance evaluations. Our findings indicate that the proposed system can effectively deliver high-bitrate video streams to thousands of users across various network environments. The source code is available at https://github.com/vidcast/vidcast.

The rapid expansion of 5G networks and the Internet of Things (IoT) is fueling a surge in video traffic, which is expected to account for over 82% of global data usage by 2022. This growth is largely attributed to the rising popularity of video streaming platforms such as YouTube, Netflix, and Facebook. Despite the deployment of high-bandwidth infrastructure, the sheer volume of video traffic continues to outpace network capacity. Furthermore, the recent global pandemic has intensified the demand for video streaming for remote work and education, further exacerbating bandwidth limitations. Consequently, developing efficient peer-to-peer (P2P) video streaming systems is critical for addressing these challenges.

While numerous P2P video streaming systems have been developed, most rely on centralized architectures that utilize a central server to distribute video segments to peers. These systems often struggle to scale effectively to large user bases. In contrast, this paper proposes a fully distributed, P2P video streaming system. We outline the system's architecture, algorithms, and implementation, and provide performance evaluations. Our results show that the proposed system can deliver high-bitrate video streams to thousands of users across different network conditions. The source code is available at https://github.com/vidcast/vidcast.

Specifically, we demonstrate that for a quadratic unramified extension $K/\mathbb{Q}$, the ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K$ is not free of rank one over its Galois group over $\mathbb{Z}$. Furthermore, if $L/\mathbb{Q}$ is a finite unramified extension with Galois group $G$, then $\mathcal{O}_L$ is free over $\mathbb{Z}[G]$ if and only if $\mathcal{O}_L$ contains no nontrivial ideal that is free over $\mathbb{Z}$. These results extend to Galois extensions of any field $k$ where the absolute Galois group is free over $\text{Gal}(-/k)$. Our approach relies on class field theory and class numbers. Additionally, we provide an explicit example of a non-abelian unramified extension $L/\mathbb{Q}$ whose ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_L$ is not free over $\mathbb{Z}[\text{Gal}(L/\mathbb{Q})]$. We argue that these errors are inherently predictable and can be systematically categorized. Large language models (LLMs) have recently been applied to proof verification and correction, yet they frequently produce mathematically incorrect results. This study provides a qualitative analysis of specific errors found in potentially incorrect outputs from an LLM attempting to correct flawed mathematical proofs. We categorize these errors into four distinct types and discuss strategies for reducing their occurrence. Our framework is designed to be general, covering a wide range of proof styles and levels of complexity. We illustrate its utility with examples from elementary number theory and graph theory. The source code for this project can be accessed at https://github.com/robertjgg2000/LLM-Proof-Error-Analysis.

While LLMs have shown promise in assisting with mathematical proofs, they often fail to correctly identify and correct errors in provided demonstrations. This research presents a framework for categorizing errors in LLM-generated outputs during the correction of flawed mathematical proofs. We apply this framework to outputs from a model tasked with correcting elementary number theory proofs. The results indicate that the model often reproduces the syntactic structure of mathematical language without fully grasping its semantic meaning. We conclude by proposing strategies to mitigate these errors

Nuclei (AGN) are expected to evolve over time due to accretion and gravitational wave emission. While these processes are well-understood for isolated systems, their impact on the broader AGN population remains uncertain. This study investigates how accretion and gravitational wave emission influence the mass and spin distributions of the most massive black holes in the local universe. We model the accretion history of AGN using a phenomenological framework that accounts for feedback mechanisms and star formation, while calculating gravitational wave emission via a semi-analytic approach. Our results indicate that, on average, the masses of the most massive local black holes have increased by approximately 10% since $z=1$, whereas their spins have decreased by roughly 20%. These shifts are primarily driven by accretion, with gravitational wave emission playing a minor role. We conclude that these evolutionary trends are detectable in current surveys of local AGN. Furthermore, we propose a method to constrain the relative contributions of accretion and gravitational wave emission to black hole evolution by analyzing the mass and spin distributions of massive black holes at low redshift. This approach could help refine our understanding of the physical processes governing AGN and the formation of massive black holes.

These platforms have become integral to daily life, particularly in disseminating news and updates. However, the ease of posting content has also led to the proliferation of fake news, which poses significant risks to society by spreading misinformation, rumors, and unverified claims. This issue is especially critical during crises, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, where false information can exacerbate public health challenges. To address this problem, this study employs a machine learning approach to detect fake news. The dataset comprises 1,000 news articles—500 authentic and 500 fabricated—related to the pandemic, collected from various sources and labeled for classification. The data was preprocessed to remove irrelevant elements like URLs, emojis, and special characters, followed by tokenization and lemmatization. For classification, the Random Forest algorithm was selected due to its superior performance in handling imbalanced datasets. The model was trained on 80% of the data and evaluated on the remaining 20%, achieving an accuracy of 98.2%, a recall of 98.2%, and an F1 score of 98.2%. These results indicate that the Random Forest algorithm is highly effective for fake news detection. The findings can assist users in identifying misinformation and help media outlets and government agencies manage the spread of false information. This research is part of a broader initiative to combat fake news, with future work planned to expand the dataset and explore additional machine learning algorithms.

These functions are constructed from coherent states of QHOs, offering a more compact representation than the conventional Fock state basis. We demonstrate that our method successfully captures the non-Gaussian characteristics of the simulated states. Furthermore, we show that the simulation of various many-body systems, including the Bose-Hubbard model, can be efficiently achieved within this framework. This work introduces a fresh perspective on simulating QHOs, potentially enhancing the efficiency of future simulations involving these systems. The variational simulation of QHOs holds promise for applications in quantum chemistry and many-body physics. Our approach is particularly advantageous for simulating interacting many-body systems on near-term quantum devices, as it requires fewer variational parameters than the standard Fock state basis. Additionally, the proposed method can be readily extended to simulate other bosonic systems, such as photons in optical cavities.

Quantum harmonic oscillators (QHOs) are fundamental components in numerous many-body models, including the Bose-Hubbard model, the Dicke model, and the Jaynes-Cummings model. These systems exhibit diverse and intriguing behaviors, such as the transition from superfluid to Mott insulator phases in the Bose-Hubbard model and the emergence of superradiance in the Dicke and Jaynes-Cummings models. While numerical simulations of these systems are typically performed using the Fock state basis, this approach becomes computationally demanding when particle numbers are large. Consequently, alternative methods for simulating QHOs are necessary. Various techniques have been developed for this purpose, including the time-evolving block decimation method, the truncated Wigner approximation, the positive $P$ representation, and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, QHOs can now be simulated on quantum computers. However, existing methods often involve complex calculations or are restricted to specific scenarios. For instance, the time-evolving block decimation algorithm is limited to one-dimensional lattices, the truncated Wigner approximation fails to capture quantum correlations, the positive $P$ representation is computationally intensive, and Monte Carlo simulations suffer from the sign problem in certain regimes. Furthermore, most of these approaches are designed specifically for many-body systems and are not applicable to single QHOs. In contrast, our proposed method can simulate both single and many-body QHOs and avoids the limitations of other techniques.

This process can either accelerate or decelerate spin rates and induce changes in the spin axis orientation. Over extended periods, these forces may cause asteroids to reach a rotational fission limit, potentially resulting in the ejection of surface material or the fragmentation of the body into a binary system. In this study, we present the first comprehensive numerical investigation into the YORP-driven fission of asteroids. We developed a computational framework that integrates the YORP torque, calculated via the ray tracing method, with the equations of motion governing the fission process. Our simulations demonstrate that the YORP effect can indeed trigger fission, with the timescale ranging from $10^6$ to $10^8$ years depending on the asteroid's size and shape. Furthermore, we identified a specific range of YORP torque directions that are most conducive to fission. These findings offer a novel perspective on the long-term rotational evolution of asteroids and provide a theoretical basis for the formation of binary asteroids through YORP-induced fission. These automata can be expressed through first-order logic formulas, denoted as $\mathsf{FO}(\cdot)$, or through regular expressions, denoted as $\mathsf{RE}(\cdot)$. This paper demonstrates that the conversion from $\mathsf{RE}(\cdot)$ to $\mathsf{FO}(\cdot)$ for infinite words is not injective, as there exist two regular expressions $r_1$ and $r_2$ such that $r_1$ and $r_2$ define the same regular function, yet $\mathsf{FO}(\cdot)$ distinguishes them. This finding contrasts with the case of regular languages over infinite words, where the equivalence of languages $L_1$ and $L_2$ implies that $\mathsf{FO}(\cdot)$ cannot distinguish them. The proof relies on the fact that the regular function computed by the concatenation of two regular expressions $r_1$ and $r_2$ depends solely on the individual functions computed by $r_1$ and $r_2$, not on the expressions themselves. Consequently, if the function computed by $r_1 \cdot r_2$ is equivalent to the function computed by $r_3 \cdot r_4$, but $r_1$ is not equivalent to $r_3$ and $r_2$ is not equivalent to $r_4$, then $r_1 \cdot r_2$ and $r_3 \cdot r_4$ compute the same regular function while being distinguishable by $\mathsf{FO}(\cdot)$. Such expressions can be constructed from those over finite alphabets, which are known to yield non-equivalent regular languages over infinite words. Furthermore, this result extends to regular languages over infinite trees, where it is established that the mapping from $\mathsf{RE}(\cdot)$ to $\mathsf{FO}(\cdot)$ is also not injective.

This study investigates the application of reservoir computing to simulate the Navier-Stokes equations governing incompressible flow past a circular cylinder at Reynolds numbers Re = 100 and Re = 200. The simulations were conducted using a spectral method on a periodic domain with dimensions $L_x = 10D$, $L_y = 20D$, and $L_z = 10D$, where $D$ represents the cylinder diameter. For Re = 100, the flow exhibits a two-dimensional vortex street in the wake, while at Re = 200, the wake becomes three-dimensional, characterized by a helical instability with a wavelength of approximately 11.3D. The computational domain was partitioned into $N_x = 128$, $N_y = 256$, and $N_z = 128$ grid points along the respective axes. To reduce computational expense, a spectral method was employed for spatial discretization, while a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme advanced the solution in time. The resulting Navier-Stokes solutions served as training data for a reservoir computer. The computer's inputs consisted of the spanwise vorticity at the cylinder surface sampled at 12 discrete $z$-locations, and its internal state was trained to reproduce velocity and vorticity fields at all grid points. At Re = 100, the trained computer successfully reproduced the von Kármán vortex street, whereas at Re = 100, it accurately simulated the three-dimensional helical flow. Furthermore, the reservoir computer was employed to forecast the temporal evolution of flow past the cylinder, achieving a prediction horizon of 200 advection time units at Re = 100 and 100 advection time units at Re = 200. The computational cost of the reservoir computer was roughly equivalent to that of the spectral solver at the surface of the cylinder, yet it was approximately 100 times faster than the solver. Consequently, the computer can be trained on a few hundred Navier-Stokes solutions and subsequently employed to simulate cylinder flow at Reynolds numbers distinct from those used during training. This approach is particularly advantageous for studying transitional flows, such as the onset of three-dimensionality at Re = 198, where the flow is inherently unstable and sensitive to initial conditions. In this framework, Eulerian advection is managed through a particle-based technique, while velocity divergence removal and Lagrangian advection are handled using particle methods. We present two variants for the remaining Eulerian steps: one employs a standard projection method, whereas the other utilizes a pressure-Poisson equation solved via a fast multipole method. This study investigates whether VTC populations encode object size and if this representation impacts the pattern of animacy specialization. We collected naturalistic eye-tracking data from participants viewing images of animals and non-animals while varying object size. Our findings indicate that VTC populations do represent object size, and that this representation is linked to the emergence of the "size effect"—a phenomenon where the difference in activation between animals and non-animals diminishes at larger scales. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this effect is driven by the presence of animals in the fovea, suggesting that the size effect arises from a reduced capacity to detect animals at peripheral visual locations. These results highlight the necessity of controlling for object size when analyzing VTC responses to animate versus inanimate stimuli. Additionally, we propose that the size effect serves as a valuable tool for probing the functional organization of VTC. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for understanding the computational processes that give rise to the animacy specialization of VTC. Eye tracking data were gathered at the University of Chicago, and fMRI data were acquired at the University of Pennsylvania. We identify that the initial surge in cases during the first epidemic wave was caused by a series of gatherings in Northern Ireland, while a subsequent rise in the second wave stemmed from a single event in London. By integrating these findings with epidemiological modeling, we conclude that super-spreader events were responsible for approximately 20% of all infections in the UK during the first wave and roughly 40% in the second wave. These findings underscore the critical necessity of implementing strict measures to prevent large-scale gatherings to effectively control the spread of the virus. Furthermore, we observe that the proportion of infections originating from super-spreader events increased as the epidemic progressed, a trend that may be linked to the adoption of mask-wearing and social distancing protocols. These behaviors likely reduced the frequency of smaller, dispersed infections, thereby elevating the relative significance of larger, concentrated outbreaks. Our results provide a rationale for the higher infection rates witnessed in the second wave compared to the first, despite the emergence of a more transmissible variant. Ultimately, our analysis highlights the pivotal influence of super-spreader events on the trajectory of the epidemic in the UK.

This study introduces a novel approach to address the sign problem by decomposing the random sign into a slowly fluctuating component and a rapidly oscillating one. By applying Monte Carlo methods to simulate the slowly fluctuating part, we can significantly reduce the rate of sign flips. This technique is demonstrated for the SU(N) Hubbard model on a honeycomb lattice, where the sign problem is eliminated for N greater than 2.5 through this decomposition method. Furthermore, the reduction in the sign problem is achieved without increasing computational costs or compromising the reliability of Monte Carlo estimations. Consequently, this work offers a practical and effective strategy for mitigating the sign problem in various many-body simulations.

This paper investigates the decidability of determining whether $Inv(\sigma)$ is infinite. We establish that this problem is undecidable in general. Furthermore, if $\sigma$ is injective, we demonstrate that $Inv(\sigma)$ is infinite if and only if it contains a square, and we show that deciding the existence of a square within the image of $\sigma$ is undecidable. Consequently, for injective code morphisms, the problem of deciding whether $Inv(\sigma)$ is infinite is also undecidable. These findings extend to the case where $\sigma$ is a power morphism. Additionally, we present an algorithm to decide if $Inv(\sigma)$ contains a square for code morphisms $\sigma$. This result was previously obtained by M. Lothaire and S. This study investigates whether RL planning mechanisms can be directly implemented within neural networks. We trained a recurrent neural network (RNN) on a hierarchical RL environment and applied spectral analysis to its activity patterns to uncover a planning algorithm. Our findings indicate that RNN activity is structured hierarchically, with lower-level units encoding immediate actions and higher-level units representing future goals.
